title: How to use AI for teaching work
description: Prepare material from current sources, explain a topic at the level your students are actually at, and keep on top of feedback and admin.
introduction: Teaching a topic you know well still takes a whole evening to prepare, because the work is not recalling the material. It is finding a current example, deciding which of the four explanations will land with this particular group, and building something that matches the specification they will actually be assessed on.

Strawberry can take the searching and assembling part. It works in the browser, so it can pull current material from real sources, work against your own curriculum or set texts rather than a generic version of the topic, and keep the link and date beside anything you will stand up and present as fact.

blocks.text: Not sure where to start? Tell your companion what you are teaching and to whom, and it can suggest a useful first step.

skill.context: Help me prepare what I am teaching next.

sections.title: Pitch it at the right level

blocks.text: The usual failure is material that is accurate and aimed slightly past the room. Ask for an explanation of a topic and most tools give you the canonical one, which is often the version written for people who already understand it.

It is more useful to get several: an analogy, a worked example, and the misconception students reliably arrive with. You know which will land with your group; the work you want taken off your plate is producing all three.

Material presented to a class carries your authority behind it, so a fabricated statistic is a different kind of problem than it is elsewhere. Strawberry keeps the link and date beside each claim, and it will not invent a source to complete a slide.

items.title: Teach into an unfamiliar field
items.text: Get the main positions, key sources, and current debates before you build the course.

skill.context: Map this subject area before I build the material.

items.title: Turn it into something teachable
items.text: Move from prepared material to slides sequenced by what students need to understand first.

skill.context: Turn this lesson into presentable material.

blocks.text: Marking is slow because writing the comment takes longer than forming the judgment. Your companion can work from your rubric to draft comments you edit, show patterns across a whole set of work, and flag where you have applied a criterion inconsistently between the first script and the twentieth.
It does not assign the grade. That stays yours, and so does the judgment behind it.

Student work is personal data, so this only runs on scripts you are authorized to process, and on de-identified copies wherever names are not actually needed. Nothing identifiable is kept beyond the task, carried into a saved skill, or used as an example when marking somebody else.

sections.title: Stay on top of the term

items.title: Catch what you owe
items.text: The commitments, unanswered emails, and follow-ups to students and colleagues that have gone quiet.

skill.context: Find the follow-ups and commitments I still owe.

items.title: Write the update
items.text: A concise, accurate update when faculty, parents, or a department need one.

skill.context: Turn my current work into a concise update.

blocks.text: Teaching material has a strange lifecycle. You build it once under pressure, use it, and then rebuild most of it a year later because the thinking behind it lives in your head rather than in the file.

Once a module works, the level you pitched it at, the sources you trusted, the structure, and the way you give feedback can all be saved. Next year starts from that. If your department teaches the same course from different rooms, that accepted approach can be shared so nobody rebuilds it in parallel.

items.context: Turn this teaching approach into something the department can reuse.

blocks.text: Watching a syllabus area, a journal, or an exam board for material worth teaching can become a Routine once you know what you actually want flagged.
